stem: What is manufacturing (factory) profit?

options.content: Market value of goods transferred less their cost of production
options.rationale: Correct: it measures how much cheaper the factory is than the market.

options.content: The difference between sales and the cost of sales of finished goods
options.rationale: That is gross profit, found in the trading account.

options.content: The profit made on raw materials that the factory resells
options.rationale: Materials that are resold are not part of the factory profit.

options.content: The profit of the whole business before tax is deducted
options.rationale: That is the profit for the year.

explanation: Manufacturing profit = transfer value − cost of production.

stem: Goods are transferred from the factory to the trading account at cost of production. What is the effect?

options.content: No manufacturing profit and no provision
options.rationale: Correct: the transfer value equals the cost.

options.content: There is a manufacturing profit but no provision is needed
options.rationale: Without a mark-up there is no profit to provide for.

options.content: There is a provision but no manufacturing profit
options.rationale: A provision only arises when there is an unrealised profit.

options.content: The trading account must not be prepared
options.rationale: The trading account is still prepared.

explanation: A transfer at cost leaves no profit in the transferred goods.

stem: Goods with a cost of production of US\$75,000 are transferred to the trading account at a market value of US\$93,750. What is the manufacturing profit?

options.rationale: This is the transfer value, not the profit.
This is the cost of production.
The cost must be deducted, not added.

explanation: Manufacturing profit = 93,750 − 75,000 = 18,750, a 25% mark-up on cost.

stem: Goods are transferred at cost plus a mark-up of 25%. Closing finished goods at transfer price are US\$60,000. What is the provision for unrealised profit?

options.rationale: This uses 25% of the transfer price instead of 25/125.
This is the cost of the closing inventory.
This halves the percentage without justification.

explanation: Profit in the inventory = 60,000 × 25 ÷ (100 + 25) = 12,000 (the cost is 48,000).
hints: The inventory already includes the mark-up.

stem: Goods are transferred at cost plus 20%. Closing finished goods at transfer price are US\$36,000. At what amount are they shown in the statement of financial position?

options.rationale: This ignores the provision for unrealised profit.
This deducts 20% of the transfer price instead of 20/120.
The provision is deducted, not added.
Correct: 36,000 less the provision of 6,000 = cost of 30,000.

explanation: Provision 36,000 × 20/120 = 6,000, so inventory is shown at cost, 30,000.
hints: Find the provision with m ÷ (100 + m).

stem: In a year the provision for unrealised profit falls because closing finished goods are lower than the opening figure. How is the decrease treated?

options.content: It is deducted from profit in the statement of profit or loss
options.rationale: A deduction is made for an increase.

options.content: It is added to profit in the statement of profit or loss
options.rationale: Correct: some profit previously held back has been realised.

options.content: It is added to the cost of production
options.rationale: The provision adjusts profit, not cost.

options.content: It is ignored because the provision is a balance sheet item
options.rationale: The change in the provision is a charge or credit to profit.

explanation: A decrease means that less unrealised profit remains, so profit is increased.
hints: Is more or less profit being held back?

stem: Why is a provision for unrealised profit created?

options.content: The factory has made a loss on the goods transferred
options.rationale: A loss is not what the provision deals with.

options.content: Customers may return the goods and ask for refunds
options.rationale: Returns are handled by returns inwards.

options.content: The closing inventory includes profit not yet earned
options.rationale: Correct: prudence requires the profit to be removed until the goods are sold.

options.content: Inventory may lose value because of damage or theft
options.rationale: Damage is covered by valuing at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

explanation: Profit is earned when goods are sold; the provision removes the profit in unsold goods.
hints: Think about when profit is earned.

stem: Goods are transferred at cost plus 25%. Finished goods at transfer price were US\$40,000 at the start of the year and US\$55,000 at the end. What is the effect of the provision for unrealised profit on profit for the year?

options.content: Profit is increased by US\$3,000
options.rationale: An increase in the provision reduces profit.

options.content: Profit is reduced by US\$11,000
options.rationale: Only the change in the provision is charged, not the full closing provision.

options.content: Profit is reduced by US\$3,000
options.rationale: Correct: the provision rises from 8,000 to 11,000, an increase of 3,000.

options.content: Profit is reduced by US\$8,000
options.rationale: The opening provision was charged in an earlier year.

explanation: Opening 40,000 × 20% = 8,000; closing 55,000 × 20% = 11,000. The increase of 3,000 is deducted.
hints: Find the opening and closing provisions.

stem: Only the change in the provision for unrealised profit is shown in the statement of profit or loss each year.
explanation: True. The provision is a balance carried forward; each year only the increase or decrease affects profit.

stem: A transfer at market value means that the total profit of the business over its whole life is higher than if goods were transferred at cost.
explanation: False. The method only splits the same profit between the factory and the shop; the provision prevents profit being counted early.
hints: Is the manufacturing profit realised before the goods are sold?

stem: Match each item with its meaning or treatment.

left.content: Closing finished goods in the statement of financial position

right.content: Deducted from profit for the year
Transfer price less the provision, which is cost
Transfer value less cost of production
Profit in transferred goods that are not yet sold

explanation: These four ideas fit together: profit, what is unrealised, and how it is removed.

stem: Complete the statements about the provision for unrealised profit.

payload.template: Closing finished goods are valued at {{blank:a}} price in the trading account. The provision is based on closing inventory, and an {{blank:b}} in the provision reduces profit. In the statement of financial position, inventory is shown at {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Transfer price in the trading account; an increase reduces profit; cost in the statement of financial position.

stem: Goods with a cost of production of US\$96,000 are transferred at cost plus 25%. Calculate the manufacturing profit.
Goods are transferred at cost plus 30%. Closing finished goods at transfer price are US\$45,500. Calculate the provision for unrealised profit.
The provision for unrealised profit was US\$8,400 at the start of the year and is US\$11,200 at the end. By how much is profit reduced?
explanation: 11,200 − 8,400 = 2,800, the increase in the provision.
hints: Compare the closing provision with the opening one.

stem: Cost of production US\$140,000; goods are transferred at cost plus 25%. Sales US\$245,000; opening finished goods at transfer price US\$30,000; closing US\$40,000; other expenses US\$31,000. Calculate the profit for the year after the provision adjustment.
explanation: Manufacturing profit 35,000; transfer value 175,000. Cost of sales 30,000 + 175,000 − 40,000 = 165,000. Gross profit 80,000. Provision opening 6,000, closing 8,000: increase 2,000. Profit 80,000 + 35,000 − 2,000 − 31,000 = 82,000.
workedSolution: 1. Manufacturing profit 35,000; transfer value 175,000. Cost of sales 30,000 + 175,000 − 40,000 = 165,000. Gross profit 80,000. Provision opening 6,000, closing 8,000: increase 2,000. Profit 80,000 + 35,000 − 2,000 − 31,000 = 82,000.
hints: Find the transfer value, the gross profit, the manufacturing profit and the change in the provision.

stem: Name the type of profit that is included in unsold finished goods transferred from the factory at market value.
explanation: It is unrealised profit because it has not yet been earned by a sale.

stem: Explain why a business might transfer goods from its factory at market value instead of at cost.

points.description: It allows the factory's cost to be compared with the price of buying the goods from outside
The performance of the factory and the shop can be measured separately
It helps decide whether to continue making the goods or to buy them

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Transferring at market value lets the owner compare the factory's cost with the market price, judge the factory and the shop separately, and decide whether to carry on manufacturing or to buy the goods.

explanation: One mark each for comparison, separate performance and the decision.
hints: What does the manufacturing profit tell the owner?

stem: Explain why the provision for unrealised profit is needed and where it appears in the financial statements.

points.description: Closing inventory is valued at transfer price, which includes profit not yet earned
Prudence: profit should be recognised only when the goods are sold
The change in the provision goes through the statement of profit or loss and the provision is deducted from inventory in the statement of financial position

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Closing finished goods are at the transfer price, including profit not yet earned. Prudence says profit is earned on sale, so a provision removes it: the change goes through the statement of profit or loss and the provision is deducted from inventory in the statement of financial position.

explanation: One mark each for the reason, prudence and the two places.
hints: Think about when profit is earned.

stem: The manager of a factory says: "We made a manufacturing profit of US\$40,000, so our factory is efficient." Evaluate this statement.

points.description: A manufacturing profit shows the factory's cost is below the transfer price used
The transfer price (mark-up) is chosen by management and may not equal the true market price
Part of the profit is unrealised if goods are unsold
Conclusion: it is evidence of efficiency only if the market value is reliable and compared with outside prices

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A manufacturing profit means the factory's cost is below the transfer price, but management chooses the mark-up, so it may not match the market price, and part of the profit is unrealised until goods are sold. It shows efficiency only if the market value is reliable.

explanation: A balanced answer questions the reliability of the transfer price and the unrealised element.

stem: Gweru Gates makes metal gates. For the year ended 31 December 2025 the cost of production was US\$84,000. Goods are transferred to the trading account at cost plus 25%. Sales were US\$150,000. Finished goods at transfer price: opening US\$20,000, closing US\$30,000. The opening provision for unrealised profit is based on the same mark-up. Other expenses were US\$18,000.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit needed at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: By how much does profit fall because of the change in the provision?

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Prepare the extract of the statement of profit or loss from gross profit to profit for the year.

points.description: Gross profit 55,000
Add manufacturing profit 21,000
Less increase in provision for unrealised profit 2,000
Less other expenses 18,000 and profit for the year 56,000

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Gweru Gates: extract from the statement of profit or loss**

|  | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Gross profit | 55,000 |
| Add manufacturing profit | 21,000 |
| Less increase in provision for unrealised profit | (2,000) |
| Total | 74,000 |
| Less other expenses | (18,000) |
| **Profit for the year** | 56,000 |

explanation: This item practises manufacturing profit and an increase in the provision.
hints: Value both inventories at transfer price.

Other expenses were US\$31,000.

parts.stem: Calculate the value of goods transferred to the trading account.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the provision for unrealised profit

Manufacturing profit 50,400 added

The decrease of 3,000 is added to profit because profit held back earlier has been realised by sales

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Closing finished goods are lower than the opening figure, so less unrealised profit remains. The decrease of US\$3,000 is added to profit because profit held back earlier has now been realised.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Suggest one reason why the manager should be careful about judging the factory by its manufacturing profit.

points.description: The mark-up of 40% is set by the business and may differ from real market prices
Part of the profit depends on goods being sold; the factory's efficiency should be checked against outside prices

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The 40% mark-up is set by the business and may not equal the real market price, so the manufacturing profit should be checked against outside quotations.
